In a major protective function it is proposed to act as a 'redox switch' in the activation-inactivation of cellular growth factors and other functional proteins; growth inhibition is generally achieved by selenium-mediated stimulation of cellular respiration (more oxygen, less cancer). Selenium appears to inhibit tumor-virus replication and oncogene activation by similar mechanisms, and may also alter carcinogen metabolism and protect DNA against carcinogen-induced damage. It further acts as an acceptor of biogenic methyl groups, is involved in detoxification of metals and certain xenobiotics, and has immunopotentiating properties.

The anchored verbatim spells it correctly TWICE ("Gd - Gadolinium, a Rare Earth" and "land animals accumulate gadolinium in bone and liver"), and no "Gadolium" spelling appears anywhere in the +/-3500-char span. The parenthetical injects a source-defect that the provided source does not contain. Every other element checks out: 5.4 ppm igneous, up to 70 ppm land plants, bone/liver rapid accumulation after absorption, and the absence of a deficiency disease are all faithful to the verbatim.
unverified_flag_detail.proposed_edit: In Rare Earths: Forbidden Cures, Wallach catalogs gadolinium -- a rare-earth metal -- in his periodic-table survey. His entry records its natural distribution (5.4 parts-per-million in igneous rocks down to trace levels, up to 70 parts-per-million in land plants) and notes that land animals accumulate gadolinium in bone and liver very quickly after absorption. He records no specific deficiency disease here; the value is completeness -- this is gadolinium's second sourced appearance alongside the Epigenetics catalog, confirming Wallach counts it among the rare-earth minerals taken up by living tissue.
